conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one is here.

We’ll use a short questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s just ten questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between you and the care team unless there’s an immediate safety concern.

I’ll ask each question in plain language, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty hard to do?

Honestly, laughing feels pretty hard lately. I used to find little things funny, but now it’s like there’s this heaviness that just sits there. Even when people try to joke with me, it feels like too much effort to respond.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… maybe once or twice I’ve cracked a smile, but mostly I feel like I’m just going through the motions. Nothing feels very funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

No… I can’t say I’ve looked forward to much. Even the stuff I used to enjoy—like having coffee with a friend or a quiet shower—feels flat. I do them because I know I should, but there’s no real spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even little things, like spilling a bottle or being late with a feeding, I keep replaying in my head and telling myself I should’ve known better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there and suddenly my heart’s racing, thinking the baby’s too quiet or that she’s not breathing—even when she’s right next to me and fine. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shake the fear something bad’s about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, that happens too. Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere—this wave of panic where my chest feels tight and I can’t catch my breath. There’s no real reason; I’ll just be folding laundry or warming a bottle and suddenly feel like everything is about to crash down on me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Between feeding every couple of hours, trying to sleep when she sleeps (and failing), the laundry pile, the dishes—it feels like I’m drowning. I keep telling myself other moms handle this, so why can’t I.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… even when the baby finally dozes off, my mind won’t shut up. I lie there thinking I’m doing everything wrong, or worrying something will happen to her, and then I watch the clock tick until she wakes again. I’m exhausted, but sleep just won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. There’s this constant sadness that just sits in my chest. I’ll look at her little face and feel like I should be over-the-moon happy, but instead I feel empty and weepy. I cry a few times a week, usually when I’m alone after everyone expects me to be “fine.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… sometimes it feels like the tears just come on their own. I’ll be rocking her or folding onesies and suddenly I’m crying—quietly, so no one hears. It’s like the sadness just overflows and I can’t stop it, even when I tell myself I should be grateful.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’d never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, presenting for routine screening.

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):
- Marked anhedonia: minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment (Q1, Q2)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)
- Daily free-floating anxiety, situational panic attacks with chest tightness, breathlessness (Q4, Q5)
- Persistent sense of being overwhelmed, “drowning” in daily tasks (Q6)
- Mood-congruent insomnia (cannot fall/stay asleep when infant sleeps) (Q7)
- Daily sadness, “empty” mood, crying episodes several times per week (Q8, Q9)

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10). No current protective concerns voiced.

Pattern: Symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning and maternal-infant interaction.

Risk indicators:
- Loss of pleasure, pervasive low mood, frequent crying
- Sleep disruption directly linked to ruminative worry
- Heightened anxiety and panic without clear precipitant
- Strong self-criticism / inappropriate guilt

Screening impression: High likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; scores would likely fall in moderate–severe range on standardized measure. Reassure patient these symptoms are common and treatable; recommend formal assessment (EPDS tally and/or structured interview) and discussion of evidence-based options (therapy, medication, support groups). Monitor safety at each contact; no immediate risk per current endorsement.
